hints: Look at where the glycerol backbone on the left joins each fatty acid chain on the right - focus on the bridging oxygen atom.
walkthrough:
Spot Where Glycerol Meets Fatty Acid**
Think of a triglyceride as one glycerol joined to three fatty acids. In Fig. 2.1 the vertical chain on the left is glycerol and the three horizontal chains are fatty acids. The join is made by an oxygen bridge: glycerol-C - O - C(=O)-fatty acid.

Circle Only The Single Bond**
The ester bond is that C-O single bond. Do not include the C=O double bond of the carboxyl group. Circling any one of the three identical -O- links is correct.
Final answer: Circle around any one C-O single bond linking glycerol to a fatty acid (the -O- between glycerol C and fatty acid C=O).

hints: Recall the general name for joining two small molecules by removing water to make a larger molecule.
Count how many fatty acids join to one glycerol and remember one water is lost per new bond formed.
walkthrough:
Name The Building Reaction**
Joining glycerol and fatty acids removes -OH from one and -H from the other to form water and a new covalent bond. That water-removing building reaction is condensation. For lipids it is often called esterification.

Count The Bonds Equals Count The Waters**
One glycerol + three fatty acids makes three ester bonds. Each ester bond formation releases one water molecule, so $3$ water molecules are produced in total.
Final answer: type of reaction: condensation (dehydration synthesis / esterification); number of water molecules produced: three.

hints: Start from what all enzymes are chemically and where this lipase works relative to the cell that made it.
walkthrough:
Why Macromolecule And Extracellular**
All enzymes are proteins, and proteins are large polymers so they are macromolecules. This lipase is secreted by exocytosis and digests triglyceride in the intestinal lumen, outside the cell that made it, so it is an extracellular enzyme.

Why Not The Others**
It is not a fibrous protein because enzymes need a precise globular tertiary shape to form an active site. It is not a polysaccharide because it is made of amino acids, not sugars.
Final answer: macromolecule and extracellular enzyme.

hints: Find pH 6.6 and pH 6.3 on the y-axis of Fig. 2.2, read across to the curve and down to the time axis for each.
walkthrough:
Read Off Both Times**
On Fig. 2.2, pH $6.6$ meets the curve at about $2$ h. pH $6.3$ meets the curve at about $6$ h. Read carefully using the grid where each small square is $0.05$ pH units and $0.5$ h.

Subtract To Get The Interval**
Time interval = $6 - 2 = 4$ h. This is the time taken for the pH to fall from $6.6$ to $6.3$.
Final answer: time taken = $4$ h.

hints: Link what lipase does to triglyceride to what product could change pH.
Compare the steepness of the curve at the start with later - what does steep mean for rate of acid production.
Think why the rate slows - consider substrate availability and movement away from optimum pH.
Think why the curve flattens completely after 18 hours at pH 6.1.
walkthrough:
Why pH Falls**
Lipase catalyses hydrolysis of the ester bonds in milk triglyceride, producing glycerol and fatty acids. The fatty acids release H+ ions into solution, so pH falls from $8.0$ toward $6.1$.

Why Fastest At The Start**
At the start substrate concentration is highest and pH is $8.0$, which is close to the optimum for lipase. More frequent enzyme-substrate collisions give the steepest rate of acid formation and pH fall.

Why The Rate Slows**
As time passes, triglyceride is used up so substrate concentration becomes limiting and fewer collisions occur. At the same time pH falls further from the optimum, altering charges and hydrogen bonds in lipase, changing tertiary structure and active site shape, so some enzyme denatures and works more slowly.

Why It Plateaus**
After about $18$ h pH stays constant at $6.1$. No more fatty acids are being made, either because all triglyceride has been hydrolysed or because all lipase is denatured at this acidic pH.

Final answer: Lipase hydrolyses triglyceride to fatty acids and glycerol; fatty acids lower pH. Fastest fall at start when triglyceride concentration highest. Rate slows as substrate used up and as pH moves from optimum pH 8 causing lipase to denature. Plateau at pH 6.1 after 18 hours when all substrate hydrolysed or all enzyme denatured, so no further acid produced.

hints: Think how more lipase molecules at the start changes collision frequency and initial rate of fatty acid production.
Think whether the total amount of triglyceride to be digested has changed, and what that means for the final pH and time to finish.
walkthrough:
Faster Start**
With higher lipase concentration there are more active sites available at any moment. More triglyceride molecules can bind per unit time, so fatty acids are released faster and pH falls more steeply at first.

Earlier Finish But Same End Point**
Because the reaction runs faster, the fixed amount of milk triglyceride is used up sooner, so the plateau is reached earlier. The total amount of fatty acid that can be made from that milk is unchanged, so the final pH stays the same.
Final answer: Initial fall in pH more rapid; plateau reached earlier; plateau at same final pH of about 6.1.
